---
title: "GROBID"
subtitle: "Optional structured enrichment of your library — parsed references and citation links"
---

::: {.callout-note}
## You almost certainly don't need this

Flux extracts text from every PDF on its own, with no setup and no extra software. Search, the
reader, and the library all work fully without GROBID. This page is for one specific want: turning
your PDFs' **bibliographies into structured records**, and linking each in-text citation to the
entry it points at.

If that isn't something you need, close this page. Nothing else in Flux refers to it.
:::

## What it adds

[GROBID](https://github.com/grobidOrg/grobid) is a mature, Apache-2.0 tool that reads a scholarly
PDF and returns a labelled document rather than a wall of text. Where Flux gives you clean text
plus a body/bibliography split, GROBID additionally gives you:

- **references parsed into fields** — author, title, journal, year, DOI, per entry
- **in-text citation links** — which "[12]" on which page points at which entry
- **sections with their text attached**, not just a list of heading strings
- **title, authors, affiliations and abstract** as parsed fields rather than heuristics

On a 13-paper trial over a neuroscience library it parsed 1,303 references and linked 92% of 1,848
in-text citations, at about 3 seconds per paper.

It does **not** improve the running text. Measured on the same papers, GROBID's searchable text is
0.92–1.01× what Flux already extracts. Adopt it for the structure, not for the words.

## Setup

Everything below is safe to hand to an AI agent: *"read docs/integrations/grobid.qmd and set up
GROBID for me."* Each step verifies before moving on.

### 1. Check for a JDK — not just a JRE

GROBID is built from source, which needs a **full JDK**. A great many machines have only the
runtime, and the failure is confusing (`Cannot find a Java installation ... matching
languageVersion=21`), so check the compiler rather than `java`:

```bash
javac -version    # must print 21 or newer
```

If that fails, install a JDK. No root required — a portable build works fine:

```bash
curl -L -o /tmp/jdk21.tar.gz \
  "https://api.adoptium.net/v3/binary/latest/21/ga/linux/x64/jdk/hotspot/normal/eclipse"
mkdir -p ~/jdk21 && tar -xzf /tmp/jdk21.tar.gz -C ~/jdk21 --strip-components=1
~/jdk21/bin/javac -version
```

On macOS swap `linux/x64` for `mac/aarch64` (Apple Silicon) or `mac/x64` (Intel). Docker is **not**
required — it is only a convenience wrapper around this same JVM.

### 2. Clone and start the service

```bash
git clone --depth 1 --branch 0.9.1 https://github.com/grobidOrg/grobid.git ~/grobid
cd ~/grobid
JAVA_HOME=~/jdk21 PATH=~/jdk21/bin:$PATH ./gradlew run --no-daemon \
  -Porg.gradle.java.installations.paths=$HOME/jdk21
```

Drop the `JAVA_HOME`/`-P` parts if `javac -version` already worked without them. The first build
takes several minutes; the clone is ~2 GB because the models ship with it. Nothing is downloaded
afterwards — it runs entirely offline.

Leave it running and confirm from another shell:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8070/api/isalive     # -> true
```

### 3. Enrich the library

```bash
flux grobid                # coverage + is a service reachable
flux grobid --run          # enrich everything not already current
```

`--run` is incremental and resumable: papers already enriched are skipped, each is written as it
completes, and an interrupted run picks up where it stopped. Useful flags:

| flag | effect |
|---|---|
| `--limit 20` | stop after 20 papers — good for a first look |
| `--keys a,b` | only these citekeys |
| `--force` | redo papers already current, e.g. after upgrading GROBID |
| `--url …` | a service somewhere other than `http://localhost:8070` |
| `--reproject` | rebuild `grobid.json` from stored TEI. **No service needed** — used after a Flux upgrade changes the projection format |

Once enrichment is done you can stop the GROBID service. The data is on disk; Flux never contacts
it again unless you run `--run` for newly added papers.

## Where it is stored

Two files per paper, inside the item's own folder in FluxLib, plus one ledger:

```
items/<citekey>/grobid.tei.xml   GROBID's raw output, kept verbatim
items/<citekey>/grobid.json      the flattened projection Flux reads
.fluxlib/grobid.json             coverage ledger: what is enriched, stale, or failed
```

The raw TEI is kept deliberately. If a later version of Flux extracts more from the same output,
`flux grobid --reproject` re-derives every `grobid.json` in seconds without re-running the service.

`grobid.json` carries a `schemaVersion`, and the ledger records the GROBID version that produced
each item, so the two can be re-derived independently. Everything here is derived data: deleting
any of it loses nothing that cannot be regenerated from the PDFs.

## Removing it

```bash
rm -rf ~/grobid ~/jdk21
find <FluxLib>/items -name 'grobid.*' -delete
rm -f <FluxLib>/.fluxlib/grobid.json
```

Flux returns to exactly its default behaviour. No feature stops working, because none of them
depended on it.

## Known limits

- **No OCR.** A scanned, image-only PDF yields nothing — the same limit Flux's own extractor has.
- **Tables and equations are its weak spot.** GROBID locates them but reproduces their contents
  poorly; it ranks near the bottom of published table-extraction benchmarks. It is a
  bibliographic and structural tool, not a table parser.
- **About 19% of parsed references carry a DOI**, because most journals do not print DOIs in their
  bibliographies. Resolving the rest still needs a lookup.
